records.statement: Separation occurs when covariates perfectly predict a discrete outcome. Complete separation perfectly predicts every observed outcome; quasi-complete separation does so for a subset. Separation can make finite maximum-likelihood odds-ratio estimates effectively infinite.

Separation is especially associated with small or sparse datasets, rare outcomes, rare exposures, highly correlated covariates, and strong covariate effects; ordinary maximum-likelihood estimation can break down or become seriously biased under these conditions.
Penalized-likelihood approaches can prevent infinite coefficient estimates under separation and are also used to address broader sparse-data problems; Firth penalization is one such approach.
Evidence does not support a universal minimum rule of 10 events per variable for binary logistic regression; problems at low events-per-variable also depend on factors such as total sample size.
Low-events-per-variable simulations can be materially affected by separation, and different handling of separation changes conclusions about logistic-regression performance.
Firth correction can improve regression-coefficient accuracy and alleviate problems associated with separation in small or sparse binary logistic-regression settings.
